# Poko Master Engineering Plan

## Poko Master Engineering Plan

Status: Planning baseline
Audience: Moby Productions engineering team and coding agents
Primary use: Vibe coding / implementation guidance
Scope: Engine, Mute, Game Authority, Main Backend, PokoX, Poko Studio, Moderation, platform fundamentals, infrastructure, security, testing, release engineering.
Excluded from this document: detailed character/rig conversion rules and the exhaustive user-facing feature catalog. Those live in conversion.md and features.md.
Core principle: cheap by default, powerful when needed.

## 0. How To Use This Plan

This document is authoritative for architecture and implementation order until an explicit revision is approved.
Every task must have an owner, status, dependency, acceptance criteria, and test strategy before implementation.
Coding agents must prefer existing interfaces over inventing parallel systems.
Do not introduce a new persistent service when an existing module can satisfy the requirement.
Do not expose a third-party dependency directly through creator-facing APIs.
Do not make client state authoritative when the requirement belongs to the Game Authority or Main Backend.
Do not put gameplay hot paths through Cloudflare Workers unless the traffic pattern is explicitly designed for it.
When an implementation decision is ambiguous, follow the dependency direction and failure rules in this document.

## 1. Product Boundary

Poko consists of PokoX, Poko Studio, Poko Moderation, Poko Engine, Mute, Game Authority, and Main Backend.
PokoX is the player runtime and platform client.
Poko Studio is the creator/developer application.
Poko Moderation is the trust and operations application.
Poko Engine is shared runtime/editor technology.
Mute is the game programming language.
Game Authority is a lightweight request-validation authority, not a continuously simulated game server.
Main Backend is the platform control plane and persistent state owner.

## 2. System Dependency Graph

The dependency direction is:
Platform Applications -> Poko SDK/API -> Poko Engine or Backend SDK -> infrastructure.
Poko Engine -> external foundations through adapters.
Mute -> Poko Engine runtime APIs and compiler services.
Game Authority -> WebSocket protocol, Mute runtime, session state, validation, PKX.
Main Backend -> PostgreSQL/Valkey/D1/R2/external providers.
Poko Studio -> Engine runtime plus project/build services.
PokoX -> Engine runtime plus platform client services.
Moderation -> Main Backend APIs and audit systems.
Circular dependencies are prohibited at module boundaries.

## 3. Non-Goals

Do not build an internal CDN.
Do not build a replacement database.
Poko Physics is a Poko-owned engine subsystem from the first production architecture; Jolt is optional/reference-only for differential validation.
Do not expose Diligent directly; Poko RHI remains the engine-facing graphics abstraction.
Do not build a replacement Git implementation.
Do not build a global multi-region platform before APAC operation is stable.
Do not require server-side continuous physics simulation.
Do not require AAA-level rendering defaults.
Do not create dozens of microservices before operational evidence requires decomposition.
Do not create multiple scripting languages.

## 6. CI/CD Baseline

Every merge must run formatting, static analysis, unit tests, integration tests applicable to touched modules, and package validation.
Release pipelines must produce signed or integrity-protected artifacts.
PNV must be assigned by release tooling rather than manually typed.
Artifact provenance must be retained.
Failed release builds must not become published versions.

## 7. Dependency Management

External dependencies are pinned by revision and recorded in a machine-readable dependency manifest.
Use third-party foundations where they save years of work.
Wrap them behind Poko-owned adapters.
Track upstream revision, local patches, license, security notes, compatibility state, and test coverage.
Prefer upstream contributions over permanent forks.

## 8. Planned Foundation Libraries

Expected foundations include:
Jolt Physics as an optional differential/reference validation backend; Poko Physics remains the owning implementation and public API.
Diligent Engine for graphics API abstraction.
miniaudio or equivalent for audio foundation.
Tracy or equivalent for profiling during development.
meshoptimizer for mesh processing.
A glTF importer such as fastgltf for modern model import.
KTX/Basis ecosystem for GPU-friendly texture pipelines where appropriate.
zstd for general-purpose compression where appropriate.
FreeType and HarfBuzz for text/font processing.
libsodium or equivalent for cryptographic primitives where needed.
Exact versions are pinned when implementation begins and validated through CI.

## 9. Coding Standards

C/C++:
Use explicit ownership.
Prefer RAII.
Avoid hidden global state.
Use strong types for IDs and units.
Keep ABI boundaries narrow.
Do not throw across C ABI boundaries.
Use Doxygen for all code documentation and comments.
**Fine-Grained Translation Units:**
- Break implementations into small, logically grouped source files (one function or small group per file)
- Each subfolder should contain corresponding implementation files
- This enables fast incremental builds - when one file changes, only that file recompiles
- Example: `src/core/memory/allocators/system/allocate.cpp` implements allocation only
- Example: `src/core/memory/allocators/system/deallocate.cpp` implements deallocation only
- Headers should remain in `include/` with matching structure
- This applies to all engine core modules and major systems
Go:
Context propagation is mandatory for network and storage calls.
Errors are explicit.
Avoid package-level mutable state.
TypeScript:
Strict compiler settings.
Runtime validation for external input.
Kotlin:
Lifecycle-safe platform integration.
All code:
No silent failure.
No unchecked user input.
No direct provider-specific assumptions in product modules.

## 10. Logging and Diagnostics

Every executable gets structured logging.
Every request crossing a network boundary carries a request or correlation identifier.
Logs must support severity, subsystem, PNV, build ID, and timestamp.
User-facing applications expose safe diagnostics while internal services retain deeper diagnostics.
Secrets must never be logged.
Binary payload logging must be opt-in and redacted by default.

## 11. PNV Versioning

PNV is the public numeric version identity.
PNV is not a cryptographic hash.
PNV is monotonic within its version registry and never reused.
Build IDs identify an exact generated artifact.
Content hashes remain internal integrity/cache identifiers.
PNV applies to engine, Mute, Studio, PokoX, authority, PKX formats, games, packages, plugins, and other released artifacts as appropriate.
Compatibility checks compare PNV ranges or minimum supported values.
Rollback creates a new release state referencing an older artifact; it does not rewrite release history.

## 12. PNV Tooling

Create a PNV registry service or registry module.
Create PNV allocation CLI.
Create build metadata embedding.
Create artifact manifest generation.
Create compatibility validation.
Create release comparison tooling.
Create Studio display of current PNV.
Create diagnostics collection of application PNV, engine PNV, Mute PNV, game PNV, and package PNV.
Test monotonic allocation, duplicate prevention, concurrent allocation, and rollback behavior.

## 13. PKX Architecture

PKX is a structured package format with a header, manifest, version metadata, content index, dependency information, integrity metadata, and payload sections.
PKX must support random-access or section-level loading where useful.
PKX must support compressed payloads.
PKX must support streaming metadata.
PKX must remain provider-independent.
Client and Authority packages are different build products from one project.
Studio project data is editable source and is not the same thing as a published runtime package.

## 77. Mute Language Service

Mute includes its language service and autocomplete implementation as first-party compiler/runtime tooling. Studio consumes the service in-process; an optional LSP adapter may be added later for external editors. There is no required external language-server deployment or web service.
The language server is embedded in the Mute compiler runtime and operates entirely client-side.

**Architecture:**
- Language service is compiled into the Mute toolchain and exposed through a stable in-process C API for Studio integration
- The optional external-editor adapter may expose LSP/JSON-RPC, but the core service does not depend on that protocol
- Maintains persistent compiler state for incremental analysis
- Shares the same compiler pipeline as the runtime (lexer, parser, AST, name resolution, type checking)
- No cloud service, no external API calls, fully offline-capable

**Features:**
- Real-time syntax highlighting with precise tokenization
- Error and warning diagnostics with source ranges and quick-fix suggestions
- Go-to-definition and find-references across the entire project
- Type-aware autocomplete with context-sensitive suggestions
- Signature help for function calls with parameter documentation
- Hover information showing types, documentation, and inline examples
- Workspace-wide symbol search and indexing
- Code navigation across module boundaries
- Real-time type checking as you type
- Rename refactoring with scope awareness
- Inlay hints for implicit types and parameter names

**Performance Techniques:**
- Incremental parsing - only re-parse changed files
- Persistent symbol index with lazy loading
- Background type checking on modified files
- Debounced requests to avoid thrashing
- LRU cache for symbol lookups
- Optimized data structures for large projects (tries, bloom filters for prefixes)
- Memory-mapped file reading for large source files
- Concurrent symbol indexing for project startup

**Client-Side Autocomplete System:**

Autocomplete is entirely client-side with no backend dependency:
- Uses static analysis from the compiler pipeline
- Builds a symbol graph during compilation
- Maintains a trie-based index for fast prefix matching
- Ranks suggestions by:
  - Lexical distance to typed prefix
  - Type compatibility
  - Scope proximity (local before global)
  - Recent usage frequency
  - Contextual relevance (e.g., after a dot, show instance members)
- Provides fuzzy matching for typos
- Shows parameter information for function calls
- Displays return types and documentation inline
- Handles engine API completions through metadata registry
- Supports snippet expansion for common patterns

**Autocomplete Ranking Algorithm:**
```
Suggestion relevance is an implementation detail; it must remain context-aware, type-aware, and user-configurable where appropriate.
```

- prefix_match: Exact match > prefix match > fuzzy match
- type_compatibility: Exact type match > compatible type > any type
- scope_proximity: Local variables > function scope > module scope > imported
- recency: Decay based on time since last use (exponential decay)
- context_relevance: Member access after dot, property access, etc.

**No Backend Design:**
- All analysis happens in the editor process or a local subprocess
- Symbol index is built incrementally and persisted to disk
- Engine API metadata is shipped with the Mute runtime (compiled-in)
- No network calls, no API keys, no privacy concerns
- Works offline without internet connection
- Fast startup with persisted cache
- Low latency responses (<50ms for most operations)

## 78. Mute Compiler Optimization Strategy

Mute uses AOT bytecode compilation as the required production path. Optional tiered/JIT execution is an explicit later optimization project and may only ship after benchmarks prove that the added complexity materially improves supported workloads.

**Primary Approach: AOT Bytecode Compiler**

The default compilation mode is AOT bytecode compilation:
- Source → HIR → Optimized HIR → Bytecode
- Bytecode is deterministic, portable, and easy to debug
- Suitable for client/server distribution via PKX packages
- Compilation latency is a benchmarked target; establish baseline measurements before setting a hard threshold for typical files.
- Good baseline performance for most game code

**Optimization Levels:**

1. **Level 0 (Debug):**
   - Minimal optimizations
   - Preserves source mapping for debugging
   - Includes runtime bounds checks
   - No dead code elimination
   - Full diagnostics metadata

2. **Level 1 (Basic - Default):**
   - Constant folding and propagation
   - Dead code elimination
   - Simple control-flow simplification
   - Inline small functions (<10 instructions)
   - Type specialization for known types
   - Loop-invariant code motion

3. **Level 2 (Aggressive):**
   - All Level 1 optimizations
   - Advanced DCE across module boundaries
   - Loop unrolling for small fixed loops
   - Function inlining with heuristics
   - Devirtualization of virtual calls
   - Escape analysis for allocations
   - Specialized collection operations

4. **Level 3 (Release):**
   - All Level 2 optimizations
   - Whole-program analysis
   - Interprocedural optimization
   - Layout optimization for structures
   - Hot/cold code splitting
   - Stripped diagnostics metadata
   - Aggressive constant propagation

**Secondary Approach: Selective JIT for Hot Spots**

For performance-critical code paths, Mute uses a selective tiered JIT:

**Tier 1: Baseline Interpreter**
- Bytecode interpreter with minimal overhead
- Used for initial execution
- Low startup cost
- Good for rarely-executed code

**Tier 2: Baseline JIT**
- One-to-one bytecode to native code translation
- No complex optimizations
- Fast compilation (<1ms)
- Good for warm code
- Includes runtime type checks

**Tier 3: Optimizing JIT**
- Hot functions are identified by profiling counters
- Compilation after N executions (default: 1000)
- Advanced optimizations:
  - Inline caching for property access
  - Type feedback from runtime
  - Speculative optimization with deoptimization guards
  - Loop optimization
  - Register allocation
- Revert to Tier 2 if speculation fails

**Tier 4: Aggressive JIT (Optional)**
- Only for extremely hot functions (top 1%)
- Profile-guided recompilation
- Aggressive inlining
- Specialization based on observed types
- Vectorization where applicable
- May use platform-specific SIMD

**Profiling-Guided Optimization (PGO):**

- Runtime profiling collects:
  - Function call counts
  - Branch frequencies
  - Type distribution
  - Allocation patterns
  - Hot loops
- PGO data can be collected during development testing
- Used to inform AOT optimization decisions for release builds
- Stored in profile files (.pgodata) alongside source

**Incremental Compilation with Optimization Cache:**

- Cache optimized intermediate representations
- Invalidate only affected portions of the dependency graph
- Reuse optimization passes when possible
- Parallel compilation for independent modules
- Link-time optimization (LTO) for final package assembly

**Optimization Passes:**

1. **Constant Folding:** Evaluate constant expressions at compile time
2. **Constant Propagation:** Replace variables with known constant values
3. **Dead Code Elimination:** Remove unreachable code and unused assignments
4. **Control Flow Simplification:** Remove redundant branches, merge blocks
5. **Loop Invariant Code Motion:** Move loop-invariant calculations outside loops
6. **Common Subexpression Elimination:** Cache computed expressions
7. **Function Inlining:** Replace function calls with function bodies
8. **Type Specialization:** Generate specialized versions for known types
9. **Devirtualization:** Convert virtual calls to direct calls when possible
10. **Escape Analysis:** Determine if allocations can be stack-allocated
11. **Loop Unrolling:** Replicate loop bodies for small fixed iteration counts
12. **Vectorization:** Convert scalar operations to SIMD where applicable (Tier 4)
13. **Register Allocation:** Assign values to CPU registers efficiently
14. **Layout Optimization:** Reorder struct fields for better cache locality

**Trade-offs:**

- AOT bytecode: predictable performance, good debugging, portable
- JIT: higher peak performance, dynamic adaptation, more complexity
- The hybrid approach gives us the best of both worlds
- JIT is opt-in via optimization level or explicit annotations
- Most game code runs well with AOT Level 2 optimizations
- Only extremely hot paths benefit from Tier 3/4 JIT

**Safety:**

- All optimization levels preserve semantic correctness
- Runtime bounds checks remain in all levels (can be disabled in Level 3)
- Deoptimization guards in JIT ensure fallback to safe execution
- No undefined behavior from optimizations
- Deterministic outputs for given inputs (except JIT profiling-based optimization)

Reject malformed manifests.
Enforce package size and dependency limits.
Prevent package path traversal.
Do not execute arbitrary native content from packages.

## 187. Plugin Security

Plugins are more privileged than game scripts.
Define capability permissions.
Show permissions during installation.
Allow disable/revocation.
Sandbox where practical.
Plugins must not silently gain new capabilities after update without review/approval policy.

## 188. Crash Handling

Every application captures safe crash context.
Include:
application PNV
engine PNV
Mute PNV where applicable
game PNV
device/OS
memory summary
thread/context
safe logs
Do not include secrets or unrestricted user content in crash payloads.

## 189. Diagnostics Transport

Diagnostics are sampled/rate-limited.
During active incidents, raise diagnostic detail through feature configuration.
Never make diagnostic volume capable of taking down the service.

## 190. Resource Budgets

Each runtime gets budgets:
CPU
GPU
memory
network
physics
script
UI
streaming
Budgets are advisory where hard enforcement would damage correctness and enforceable where safety requires it.

## 191. Dynamic Performance Policy

Dynamic performance responds to:
frame time
CPU/GPU workload
memory pressure
thermal state
device capability
Adjust expensive systems gradually.
Keep user-selected manual settings where possible unless safety requires reduction.

## 192. Mobile Optimization

Prioritize:
startup time
memory use
texture compression
shader variant reduction
asset streaming
dynamic resolution
thermal behavior
touch latency
battery-aware policies
low-memory recovery

## 193. Windows Optimization

Prioritize:
high refresh rates
controller/keyboard/mouse support
multiple display configurations
higher graphics scalability
fast SSD asset caches
advanced quality settings

## 194. Backend Optimization

Main Backend:
batch database operations
cache hot data
avoid redundant serialization
use bounded workers
separate background analytics from critical APIs
Game Authority:
zero/minimal allocation hot paths
binary decode
session-local RAM
specialized Mute execution
backpressure

## 195. Vibe Coding Rules

AI coding agents must:
read local module contracts
preserve architecture
add tests with behavior changes
avoid broad rewrites
prefer small compilable increments
update interface documentation when APIs change
never introduce hidden provider coupling
mark TODOs with subsystem/task IDs
never claim a benchmark passed without actually running it

Task IDs use prefixes:

BACK

\n# 197. Final Architecture Corrections and Production Additions
\nThis final pass supersedes conflicting older wording in the plan. The rules in this section are binding for implementation.\n\n## 270.1 Production-first repository contract\n\nThe repositories may begin with incomplete modules, but every directory created for a subsystem must correspond to the final intended ownership boundary. Do not create temporary `prototype/`, `experimental/`, or `new2/` module trees and later depend on them.\n\nEach C/C++ library must have: a public include root, private source root, unit tests, benchmarks where performance matters, and a CMake target with a stable logical name. Each Go package must expose an explicit package boundary and avoid reaching into infrastructure adapters from domain logic. Each TypeScript Worker/DO module must keep request parsing, domain calls, and provider adapters separable.\n\n## 270.2 Canonical source-of-truth rule\n\nFor each data contract, exactly one module owns the canonical definition. Generated copies are outputs, not alternate sources. This applies to:\n\n- Engine metadata\n- Mute builtins and type metadata\n- network packet schemas\n- PKX section schemas\n- PNV compatibility records\n- backend API contracts\n- database schema definitions\n- capability declarations\n- Studio property/editor metadata\n- achievement definitions\n- marketplace item state machines\n\nA schema change must update the source and regenerate consumers in the same change.\n\n## 270.3 Reference game requirement\n\nA small but real reference game is required before declaring the runtime stack integrated. It must exercise:\n\n- Instance creation and parenting\n- Mute gameplay code\n- client UI\n- input\n- animation\n- physics\n- audio\n- network replication\n- authority validation\n- player save data\n- achievement awarding\n- reconnect\n- package loading\n- Studio playtest\n\nThe reference game is not a product feature. It is a permanent integration fixture used by CI, performance tests, and release qualification.\n\n## 270.4 Golden fixture policy\n\nEvery format with compatibility obligations gets golden fixtures checked into dedicated test data directories. A fixture must include expected parse/compile/serialize behavior and, where useful, a corruption variant. Golden fixtures must be versioned independently from generated build caches.\n\nRequired fixture classes include Mute source/bytecode, PKX packages, network packets, account/service API payloads, migration snapshots, and canonical converted character assets.\n\n## 270.5 Compatibility window policy\n\nRuntime readers must be able to reject unsupported versions deterministically. Readers must never guess a newer schema. Writers must emit one declared version and must not silently change the meaning of an existing field.\n\nThe release system maintains explicit compatibility windows for:\n\n- previous client PNVs\n- previous Studio PNVs\n- active game PNVs\n- authority package PNVs\n- protocol versions\n- Mute bytecode versions\n- persistent data schema versions\n\n## 270.6 Data migration policy\n\nDatabase migrations are forward, versioned, idempotent, and observable. Destructive migrations require a backup/restore test in staging before production approval. Long migrations must be split into expand/backfill/contract stages. Application code must tolerate the transitional schema during the migration window.\n\nMigration commands must support dry-run, checksum verification, lock/timeout controls, resumability where feasible, and explicit rollback guidance.\n\n## 270.7 Transaction policy\n\nThe platform ledger, ownership mutations, marketplace purchases, moderation state changes, and other durable cross-record actions use explicit transaction boundaries. Exactly-once delivery is not assumed from transport alone; idempotency keys and unique constraints are the durable safety net.\n\nA transaction must identify its domain owner, durable write set, idempotency key rules, retry behavior, and observable outcome.\n\n## 270.8 Cache correctness policy\n\nValkey/cache entries are disposable. Every cached record needs:\n\n- an owner\n- a key namespace\n- expiration policy\n- invalidation trigger\n- rebuild path\n- stale-read policy\n\nNo authoritative rule may depend on a cache entry existing. Cache failure should degrade latency/features before it corrupts durable state.\n\n## 270.9 External provider adapter policy\n\nProvider clients live behind Poko-owned interfaces. Each adapter translates provider errors into a Poko error taxonomy. Provider-specific status codes may be retained in diagnostics but may not become business logic conditions outside the adapter.\n\nEvery critical provider has an outage test or controlled failure simulation. Provider replacement must require implementing the same interface and passing the same contract suite.\n\n## 270.10 Host lifecycle policy\n\nEvery Game Authority host has an explicit lifecycle:\n\n```text\nREGISTERING -> READY -> DRAINING -> OFFLINE -> REMOVED\n```\n\nSessions have their own lifecycle and never infer host health solely from a TCP connection. Host Agent heartbeats, capacity counters, graceful drain, crash detection, join-ticket expiry, and removal are separate state transitions.\n\n## 270.11 Game update policy\n\nA published game version is immutable. Updating a game creates a new PNV. Existing sessions remain pinned to their loaded version until they drain or terminate. Clients never receive a partially updated package set.\n\nPublish must be atomic at the release registry level: either the client/authority package pair and metadata are fully registered, or the version remains unpublished.\n\n## 270.12 Studio recovery policy\n\nStudio must maintain crash-recoverable project state through journaled changes or periodic atomic snapshots. Autosave must never overwrite the last known-good project with a malformed state without retaining a recovery point.\n\nUndo/redo and recovery use the same command/transaction vocabulary, so a change can be replayed, undone, serialized, and audited consistently.\n\n## 270.13 PokoX update policy\n\nUpdates are staged. PokoX validates download size, integrity, manifest compatibility, disk space, and rollback availability before replacing the active installation. The updater must survive interruption without leaving the product unlaunchable.\n\n## 270.14 Moderation evidence policy\n\nModeration cases keep immutable references to the evidence used for a decision. Evidence access is capability-controlled, audited, and separated from ordinary user-facing profile data. Retention rules must be explicit.\n\n## 270.15 Privacy/data minimization policy\n\nCollect the minimum telemetry required for reliability, abuse prevention, product analytics, and operational diagnostics. The plan distinguishes operational logs, security audit records, gameplay analytics, crash telemetry, and user-generated content. Each class gets ownership, access rules, retention, and redaction behavior.\n\n## 270.16 Secrets and build provenance\n\nBuilds must record source revision, dependency revisions, toolchain identity, build configuration, PNV, and artifact digest. Signing keys are external to the source tree and injected by the release system. Development builds must be distinguishable from production builds in diagnostics.\n\n## 270.17 Feature flag policy\n\nFeature flags are configuration, not architecture. Flags need owner, default, rollout scope, expiry/cleanup ticket, and emergency-disable behavior. Long-lived flags require an explicit reason. Business rules must not multiply into nested flag combinations without a test matrix.\n\n## 270.18 Performance budget policy\n\nEvery major runtime subsystem has a target and an observed baseline. Budgets are recorded as measurable quantities such as milliseconds/frame, allocations/frame, bytes/player, MB/package, p95/p99 request latency, CPU/session, memory/session, or GPU memory.\n\nA feature that exceeds its declared budget may still ship only with an explicit budget exception and a follow-up task.\n\n## 270.19 Error taxonomy\n\nErrors are classified as:\n\n```text\nINVALID_INPUT\nNOT_FOUND\nUNAUTHORIZED\nFORBIDDEN\nCONFLICT\nRATE_LIMITED\nTEMPORARILY_UNAVAILABLE\nDEPENDENCY_FAILURE\nDATA_CORRUPTION\nINTERNAL_FAILURE\nVERSION_UNSUPPORTED\nRESOURCE_EXHAUSTED\n```\n\nSubsystems may define finer-grained codes while preserving the stable category. User-facing applications map internal errors into safe messages without exposing secrets, stack traces, provider payloads, or internal paths.\n\n## 270.20 Final implementation-order rule\n\nThe preferred order is:\n\n```text\nBuild/CI/Contracts\n  -> Core runtime primitives\n  -> Mute front end/runtime\n  -> Renderer/Physics/Audio/Input/Animation/UI foundations\n  -> Networking/PKX/Streaming\n  -> Game Authority\n  -> Studio creator workflow\n  -> PokoX platform shell\n  -> Backend/social/economy/marketplace/moderation integration\n  -> Security/recovery/scale gates\n  -> AA improvements\n```\n\nA lower layer may be incomplete while a higher layer is prototyped, but higher-level production behavior must not lock in a temporary lower-level interface.\n\n# 198. Concrete Repository File Map\n\nThe paths below are planned production paths. Creating the file is part of the task; replacing these with differently named parallel modules requires a plan revision.\n\n## 271.1 Engine 199. Cross-System Contract Tests\n\nCross-system tests are not optional integration polish. They are the place where the plan proves that independently owned modules actually compose.\n\nRequired contract suites:\n\n1. Mute -> Engine metadata\n2. Studio -> Engine metadata -> Properties\n3. Studio -> Mute language service\n4. Client -> PokoNet -> Authority\n5. Authority -> Mute -> Engine definitions\n6. PKX builder -> PKX loader\n7. Host Agent -> Backend host registry\n8. PokoX -> session allocation -> PKX manifest -> Authority join\n9. Backend -> PostgreSQL/Valkey provider adapters\n10. Marketplace -> ledger -> ownership -> inventory\n11. Moderation -> restrictions -> client enforcement\n12. Character converter -> runtime character -> animation/physics\n\nEvery suite has success, malformed-input, timeout, dependency-failure, version-mismatch, and retry cases where applicable.\n\n# 200. Release Trains\n\nUse release channels:\n\n```text\ncanary -> internal -> staging -> production\n```\n\nEngine, Mute, Studio, PokoX, Authority, and packages may promote independently, but a release that changes a cross-system contract must publish a compatibility record before promotion.\n\nA release train is blocked by:\n\n- failing golden fixtures\n- package signature/integrity failure\n- migration failure\n- critical crash regression\n- unbounded memory growth\n- p99 latency above the agreed gate without an exception\n- protocol incompatibility\n- unresolved security-critical finding\n\n# 201. Operational Readiness Review\n\nBefore the 5k-CCU milestone, operations must demonstrate:\n\n- host registration and drain\n- authority crash replacement\n- reconnect\n- package cache recovery\n- backend dependency degradation\n- database restore test\n- audit log continuity\n- incident diagnostics\n- release rollback\n- PokoX update rollback\n- Studio autosave recovery\n- provider replacement test for at least one critical storage path\n\n# 202. Final Traceability Rule\n\nEvery user-facing feature must trace to:\n\n```text\nfeature\n -> public contract\n -> owning subsystem\n -> source files\n -> unit/integration test\n -> benchmark or abuse test when relevant\n -> milestone gate\n -> release artifact\n```\n\nAnything that cannot be traced through this chain remains planning-only and cannot be called production-ready.\n\n# 203. Detailed Implementation Backlog\n\nThe following task cards are the executable backlog. They are intentionally granular enough for a coding agent to pick up one task without inventing a subsystem architecture.\n\nTask status starts at `TODO`. A task may move to `IN_PROGRESS` only after its dependencies are satisfied. `TESTED` means the implementation and its focused test have actually run. `PRODUCTION_READY` requires the release gate for the owning subsystem.\n\n# 204. First Implementation Slice

The first code should start with the Engine repository, but not by jumping directly into rendering. The first slice is deliberately small and gives every later subsystem a real build/test contract.

```text
BUILD-001..010
  -> CORE-011..020
  -> MEM/JOB/PLAT in parallel
  -> MUTE front end/runtime in parallel once compiler interfaces are frozen
```

The first playable vertical slice should be: `Workspace -> Part -> Mute script -> Input -> Physics query -> Renderer -> Studio playtest`. Do not wait for the complete backend, marketplace, social graph, or moderation product to begin engine implementation. Those systems come after the runtime contracts are stable.

# 205. Task Dependency Graph

The task list is ordered by subsystem groups above, but implementation dependencies are expressed explicitly rather than assuming numeric order. The minimum critical path is:

```text
BUILD -> CORE -> MEM/JOB/PLAT -> MUTE -> REN/PHY/ANI/AUD/UI/INPUT -> ASSET/STREAM/NET -> PKX -> AUTH -> HOST/BACK -> STU/POKOX/MOD -> SCALE/SEC/REL
```

Parallel work is encouraged where public contracts are already frozen. When two tasks touch the same canonical schema, the schema-owning task blocks downstream consumers until its generated outputs and compatibility fixtures exist.

- Use the existing canonical schema/metadata/protocol instead of inventing a parallel representation.
- Make timeout, retry, version mismatch, authorization failure, and dependency outage behavior explicit.
- Preserve idempotency for durable mutations and pin immutable versions for runtime artifacts.

Tests:
- Add positive and negative contract tests at both sides of the boundary.
- Add a version-mismatch fixture and a dependency-failure simulation where applicable.

Acceptance:
- Cross-system test passes and the involved artifacts can be inspected without special manual state.
- No provider-specific API or temporary prototype path is required for the feature to function.
Run: `python ops/validate_release.py`
Exit artifact: boundary implementation + contract fixture + diagnostic coverage.

# 207. Application Language and Platform Integration

PokoX and Poko Studio use the native Poko Engine runtime through a narrow interop boundary. For the planned desktop application shell, Windows 11 Studio UI is implemented with C# and Avalonia; the engine remains C/C++. Android application integration uses Kotlin around the native engine layer. PokoX Windows and Android builds share runtime contracts while keeping platform lifecycle/UI code separate.

The application layer must never reimplement physics, rendering, Mute execution, or game object semantics in the UI language. It invokes the real Engine APIs.


# 208. Final Milestone Checklist

- [ ] Repository bootstrap reproducibly builds all production targets.
- [ ] Dependency manifest pins third-party revisions and preserves licenses/notices.
- [ ] Mute language semantics, compiler, VM, GC, language service, and bytecode format have golden fixtures.
- [ ] Poko Engine uses a single metadata registry across runtime, Mute, Studio, serialization, and networking.
- [ ] Poko Physics is owned by Poko and differential-tested against Jolt without exposing Jolt types.
- [ ] Poko Renderer/RHI hides Diligent and has deterministic resource/shader/pipeline failure behavior.
- [ ] Poko Audio hides miniaudio and has device-loss recovery plus voice-path separation.
- [ ] PokoNet uses binary hot paths with compatibility fixtures and packet limits.
- [ ] Client and Authority packages are built from one project but contain separate purpose-specific data.
- [ ] Authority is request-authoritative and does not become a continuously simulated 60 FPS server.
- [ ] Studio edits the real runtime and its viewport is not a separate simulation implementation.
- [ ] PokoX uses the same Engine runtime and has atomic update/cache recovery behavior.
- [ ] Moderation actions are capability-controlled, audited, and testable end-to-end.
- [ ] Backend durable state is PostgreSQL-owned; cache loss is recoverable.
- [ ] Developer-hosted games use the same host lifecycle and signed join-ticket contracts as Moby-hosted sessions.
- [ ] 5k CCU load/soak/recovery tests produce measurable results and an explicit bottleneck backlog.
- [ ] Release rollback, database restore, provider degradation, and Authority crash recovery are rehearsed.
- [ ] AA work begins only after A-level regression gates remain green and new performance budgets are measured.


# 209. Source Alignment

The implementation plan must remain aligned with the companion product documents without duplicating them as competing specifications.

`features.md` is the user-facing feature baseline. This plan owns the implementation architecture, file/module ownership, build/test strategy, security boundaries, and release gates for those features.

`conversion.md` is the detailed character/content conversion contract. This plan owns how the converter is built, packaged, tested, cached, and integrated into Studio and PKX. The conversion file remains the more detailed source for conversion-specific rules.

When the feature catalog changes, update traceability and task ownership here. When conversion rules change, update converter tests and package compatibility records here.

# 210. Definitive Engineering Sign-off

This file is the current master engineering plan. A task being listed does not mean it is implemented. Only repository evidence, passing tests, measured benchmarks, and milestone gates move a task out of `TODO`.

The plan intentionally allows staged implementation, but it does not allow architecture drift disguised as prototyping. The final Poko stack must preserve these core decisions:

```text
Poko-owned creator/runtime contracts
        +
third-party foundations behind replaceable adapters
        +
real shared runtime for Studio and PokoX
        +
Mute-owned compiler/VM/language service
        +
Poko-owned Physics and Networking
        +
request-authoritative lightweight Game Authority
        +
provider-independent PKX/PNV
        +
PostgreSQL durable state / disposable cache
        +
measured A -> AA performance growth
```

The first production coding effort may begin with the Engine, specifically the build/bootstrap, Core, memory, jobs, platform abstraction, and reference test harness. Rendering, Physics, and Mute then build against those real contracts rather than against throwaway prototypes.
